title: Retailers shun central Mexico produce as US cyclospora outbreak spreads, former FDA chief says | CNN
text:
Some large retailers and restaurants have stopped ​sourcing produce from a region of central Mexico linked to the expandingU.S. cyclosporiasis outbreakbecause of concerns about widespread contamination, former U.S. Food and Drug Administration Commissioner Scott Gottlieb said on ‌Monday.

An FDA investigation haslinked the outbreakto iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell restaurants sourced from privately held Taylor Farms’ operations in central Mexico. However, health officials are searching for other potential products that may be making people sick as cases continue to climb.

Widespread contamination could broaden the risk that consumers contract cyclosporiasis from imported produce. Cyclosporiasis is a parasitic disease that causes explosive diarrhea. Removing products from supply chains linked to central Mexico would mitigate those risks, Gottlieb said.

Speaking on CNBC, Gottlieb said ​multiple outbreak clusters, including in the Great Lakes region, New York and North Carolina, appeared to be potentially linked to parsley and cilantro from central Mexico, though investigators have not determined the exact ​source.

“I think everyone believes that region is suspect,” Gottlieb said. “A lot of that product’s being taken out of supply chains.”

He did not identify companies removing products, ⁠and Reuters was not immediately able to confirm which retailers may have stopped sourcing Mexican produce.

Gottlieb said weather conditions had raised the risk of contamination. Raw sewage could have reached growing areas through ​flooding, a sewage canal breach, irrigation water or overflowing portable toilets used by farm workers, he said, adding that the cause remained under investigation.

“There was some event that happened in central Mexico — we don’t know what yet — ​that led to a lot of fields probably getting contaminated,” Gottlieb said.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and Taylor Farms had no immediate comment.

Taylor Farmshas said it voluntarily suspended production of all products at its facility in central Mexico and immediately removed all potentially affected products from the marketplace when questions arose about the source of the outbreak.

The FDA said Taylor Farms agreed to remove affected produce from the market following extensive discussions. But the company did not meet an ​established 24-hour time frame for determining whether it would take voluntary action after the agency presented it with evidence, according to a source familiar with the situation.

The U.S. outbreak has resulted in 4,173 laboratory-confirmed ​cases, with health authorities aware of more than 7,400 additional suspected cases, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Gottlieb said cases were likely underreported, and that the true scope of infection was likely 10 to 20 times ‌greater than ⁠the reported case number.

“This is the largest outbreak we’ve ever seen in history of cyclospora,” he said.

Michigan on Monday reported9,253 cases, an increase of 1,077 cases since its last update on Friday. County health officials said they thought other, unidentified items were making people sick besides Taylor Farms’ lettuce from Mexico.

“Certainly, it doesn’t tell the whole story with this one recall,” said Avani Sheth, chief medical health officer in Wayne County, Michigan, which includes Detroit.

In Mexico, analysts said it was important to wait for the results of official investigations.

Mario Puente, the head of health and safety at Mexico’s CNA agricultural chamber, said the trade association was working ​closely with authorities to investigate the outbreak and improve ​preventative practices.

“I believe we must all be very ⁠cautious, both in Mexico and the U.S., and see this evaluation through to the very end,” said Raul Urteaga, a former Mexican official and founder of consulting group Global Agrotrade Advisors.

U.S. health authorities from the FDA and U.S. Department of Agriculture, as well as Mexican sanitary agency SENASICA, carry out regular inspections on site ​as well as at the border, Urteaga said.

SENASICA and major U.S. grocers and restaurant chains did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Mexican authorities said last ​week that irrigation at Taylor ⁠Farms came from certified, company-owned wells. They did not identify health issues with workers, and water samples, as well as lettuce samples, tested negative.

Mexico produces some 550,000 tons of lettuce each year, according to consultancy GCMA, of which half is exported, almost exclusively to the U.S., where it makes up some four-fifths of imported lettuce.

Just five states in central and northern Mexico produce three-quarters of Mexican lettuce. Central Guanajuato state — home to Taylor Farms’ main operations in ⁠the country — produces ​the largest portion at 28%.

GCMA Director Juan Carlos Anaya said he found it surprising that lettuce samples have not yet tested positive ​for cyclospora and that just a few cases of illness were confirmed in Mexico.

“The situation isn’t what it is in the United States, and we eat lettuce too,” he said.
